# Wobble Rush 3D — Obstacle-Course Design Research

**Methodology / source-verification note.** From this sandbox I could reach Wikipedia, official marketing sites, the GDC Vault root, and docs portals; deep primary sources (Fandom level pages, Reddit threads, Epic help, Gamasutra/GameDeveloper article bodies, YouTube transcripts) are bot-blocked or JS-gated and could not be auto-fetched. Below, each citation is tagged: **[verified-live]** = I fetched it this session and it returned real content; **[reference]** = a real, stable URL I'm confident exists but could not auto-verify the body of from here. Numeric conventions are framed as commonly-cited industry/community rule-of-thumb, not officially-published specs, because Mediatonic has not published Fall Guys' tuning constants.

**Design DNA (the through-line for all 6 sections).** Fall Guys was explicitly inspired by game shows *Takeshi's Castle*, *It's a Knockout*, and *Total Wipeout*, plus playground games (tag, British Bulldog). Lead designer Joe Walsh cited *Takeshi's Castle* / *Total Wipeout* directly. Mediatonic enforced an internal rule that **every game mode must be explainable in three words** — this is the single most important fairness principle below: every obstacle must read at a glance. **[verified-live]** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_Guys

---

## 1. Rotating sweeper obstacles

**How they work.** A horizontal beam (or set of arms) spins around a central axle at a fixed angular velocity, sweeping a circular corridor the player must cross. The player reads the arm, times their dash through the gap between passes, and recovers on the far side.

**Spin speed / feel.**
- Sweepers are tuned to *human reaction time + commit time*, not raw difficulty. The arm completes a pass across the player's lane roughly every **1.5–2.5 s** at the "fair" end; faster than ~1.2 s per lane-pass starts to feel cheap because the player can't both read and commit.
- Linear tip speed is high (the arm moves fast at the radius), but **angular speed is kept low and constant** so the rhythm is learnable. Variable/accelerating spin is reserved for "hard" late-course sections and is the #1 cause of "cheap" complaints.
- Fairness comes from *constancy*: a constant-velocity sweeper is a rhythm puzzle; an accelerating or randomly-reversing one is a luck check.

**Placement & gap patterns.**
- Single sweeper: place in a corridor ~6–10 m wide so the player can stand off-axis and watch one full revolution before committing. The "safe pocket" (arc between arm and wall) should be ≥ ~120° so a well-timed entry has a real window.
- **Stacked/overlapping sweepers** (Fall Guys' *Whirlygig*-style): two arms on the same axle offset by ~120–180°, or two axles in series. The fair pattern offsets the second arm's phase so a player who clears #1 has a *predictable* window at #2 — i.e. the gap pattern is **phase-locked, not random**. Cheap = two independently-timed arms where the only solution is to camp and wait for a lucky alignment.
- Never place a sweeper immediately at a checkpoint respawn or right after a blind landing — the player needs ~1 s of read time on entry.

**Fair vs cheap, summary.** Fair = constant speed, phase-locked multi-arms, ≥120° safe pocket, entry lane gives read time, telegraphed direction (arm color/taper shows leading edge). Cheap = accelerating spin, random reversal, sub-90° pocket, blind-entry placement, arms that hit above head-height so the player can't see the gap.
**[reference]** Fall Guys Fandom level pages (e.g. *The Whirlygig*, *Slime Climb*) — bot-blocked here, but canonical community descriptions: https://fallguys.fandom.com/wiki/The_Whirlygig
**[reference]** YouTube level-design breakdowns: https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=fall+guys+whirlygig+level+design

---

## 2. Moving platforms

**Conventions.**
- **Ping-pong linear** is the default: a platform translates between two anchors on a sine/ease-in-out curve, *pausing briefly (~0.3–0.6 s) at each end*. The end-pause is the fairness mechanism — it gives a predictable embark/disembark window. Platforms that never stop moving force frame-perfect jumps and read as cheap.
- **Timed groups:** 2–4 platforms cycling in a set phase relationship. The fair pattern staggers phases so consecutive platforms arrive in a *walk-on rhythm* (player steps onto #1, rides, steps to #2 as it arrives). If all platforms sync (all arrive together / all leave together) the only solution is to rush — fine for an optional shortcut lane, unfair as the only path.
- **Spacing relative to jump distance:** static gap between platform edges ≈ **50–70% of the character's max standing-jump distance** for a "comfortable" hop; 70–90% = "risk lane"; >100% = impossible without a bounce/moving-catch. When the platform itself is moving *toward* the player, the effective gap shrinks (easier); moving *away*, it grows (harder) — tune so the worst-case (platform receding) still sits ≤ ~80% of max jump.

**Pacing rule of thumb.** A moving-platform sequence should be *passable while paused once* — i.e. a patient player who waits for alignment always succeeds; a skilled player can chain without waiting. That keeps the skill ceiling high without a luck floor.
**[verified-live]** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platform_game (genre conventions on suspended platforms / jumping between platforms)
**[reference]** Roblox Creator Docs (moving-platform / tween tutorials): https://create.roblox.com/docs

## 3. Bumpers / bounce pads

**Bumpers (knockback).**
- Spherical/domed obstacles that apply an impulse on contact, knocking the player back and (usually) slightly up. Tuned so contact is *punishing but recoverable*: knockback should push the player ~2–4 m (enough to drop them off a narrow beam or back into a sweeper zone) but **not** so far that one touch = guaranteed elimination — the recovery window is what makes it a skill check rather than a death sentence.
- Bumpers feel fair when they're **visually distinct from the floor** (different color/material, raised dome, often a highlight rim) and *static or slow-oscillating*. Fast-moving bumpers in tight corridors read as cheap.

**Bounce pads (vertical launch).**
- Apply an upward impulse launching the player to a **predictable apex height** — typically tuned so the apex sits ~0.5–1 m above the landing surface they're meant to reach, giving air-control margin.
- **Telegraphing is the whole contract:** bounce pads are universally colored bright yellow/orange or given a spring/coil visual and often a pulsing animation or arrow. A bounce pad that *looks* like floor is a troll obstacle, not a fair one. Sound cue (boing/spring) on contact reinforces the read.
- Knockback direction should follow surface normal, so a tilted pad launches at an angle the player can *see* — angle reads as trajectory.

**Fair vs cheap.** Fair bumper: visible dome, static, knockback recoverable, recovery window exists. Cheap: hidden/flat bumper, bumper on a blind landing, knockback that yeets the player off the level with no recovery input possible.
**[verified-live]** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platform_game (genre notes on springboards/trampolines as core platformer mechanics)
**[reference]** Roblox Creator Docs: https://create.roblox.com/docs

## 4. Narrow bridge, final ramp/gate/finish, and checkpoint pacing (~60–90 s course)

**Narrow bridge.**
- A beam ~1.2–1.8 m wide (≈ 0.7–1.0× character width) over a kill pit, often with a sweeper or bumper running its length. The narrowness is psychological pressure, not the actual challenge — the *moving hazard* on it is. Keep the bridge visually distinct from surrounding floor (different color) so the player reads "don't fall" instantly (the three-words rule).
- Length: ~8–15 m, long enough to force 2–3 hazard timings, short enough that one mistake doesn't erase minutes of progress.

**Final ramp / gate / finish.**
- The final stretch is almost always a **visual crescendo**: a rising ramp or a "dashes/gates" sprint toward a visible finish line/crown. Fall Guys' *Final* round convention: a single decisive challenge where the winner takes the match. For a short standalone course, mirror this — the last 10–15 m should be the most telegraphed, highest-energy, lowest-ambiguity section (a straight ramp to a bright finish arch, optionally with moving obstacles but always *readable*).
- Finish line is over-signaled: bright color, confetti/celebration VFX, distinct audio. The player must always know exactly where "done" is.

**Checkpoint pacing for 60–90 s.**
- **3–4 checkpoints** total (including start), spaced ~15–25 s of optimal play apart. The "50% mark" checkpoint is non-negotiable — losing all progress at the halfway point of an 80 s course is the most common "unfair" complaint.
- Place a checkpoint **after** every high-failure obstacle (post-sweeper, post-moving-platform-gap, post-narrow-bridge), never *before* a blind landing. Respawn should place the player facing the next obstacle with ~1 s of read time, never into immediate hazard contact.
- Difficulty curve: easy read → medium execution → optional risk shortcut → climactic final. Don't front-load the hardest obstacle; the player needs to warm up on the rhythm.

**[verified-live]** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_Guys (Final-round = winner convention; level-type taxonomy Course/Survival/Final; Creative elimination zones & checkpoints exist as authored tools)
**[reference]** Push Square interview/coverage of Mediatonic design (cited in Fall Guys Wikipedia refs): https://www.push-square.com/news/2020/08/soapbox_fall_guys_is_finally_a_battle_royale_i_actually_want_to_play

## 5. Player-metrics numbers (jump readability / fairness)

*Framing: Mediatonic has not published Fall Guys' tuning constants; the figures below are commonly-cited 3D-platformer and Fall-Guys-cloner conventions, useful as a starting tuning box, not gospel. Verify in-engine against your own character controller.*

- **Character size:** Fall Guys bean ≈ **1.8–2.0 m** tall visual, capsule collider ~0.5–0.6 m radius. Gap readability rule: a gap the player must jump should be readable as "wider than the character is tall" at a glance.
- **Run speed:** ~**5–7 m/s** for the Fall Guys feel (snappier 3D platformers like Mario 64 sit ~7–8 m/s; the bean is slightly floatier/slower). Jump distance is computed from run speed × air-time.
- **Jump height:** apex ≈ **1.5–2.5× character standing height** (~3–4 m), with **variable jump height** (hold = higher) being the genre norm since Mario 64 — this is what makes a single jump button serve both hops and clears.
- **Air control:** mid-air steering is the single biggest fairness lever. Fall Guys allows generous air control so the player can correct a misjudged jump; pure ballistic jumps (no air correction) read as cheap in a multiplayer course.
- **Jump distance → gap mapping (the core fairness table):**
  - Comfortable gap: **~50–70% of max standing-jump horizontal distance** (≈ 3–4 m at the above tuning).
  - Risk gap: **~70–90%** (≈ 4–5 m).
  - Max/desperation gap: **~90–100%** — reserve for optional shortcut lanes, never the only path.
  - >100%: impossible without a bounce pad, moving catch, or dive mechanic.
- **Coyote time + jump buffer:** ~0.1–0.15 s each. Standard platformer-fairness hygiene; near-mandatory for "fair" feel even though invisible to players.
- **Hazard timing vs reaction:** fair telegraph window ≈ **0.4–0.7 s** minimum from telegraph-appearance to hazard-active (≈ human visual reaction time + input commit). Below ~0.3 s reads as cheap.

**[verified-live]** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platform_game (jump trajectory fixed-vs-alterable mid-air; springboards; environmental kill obstacles — genre grounding for the above conventions)
**[reference]** GameDeveloper/Gamasutra design archives (bodies bot-blocked here; the venue is the canonical industry source for character-controller tuning posts): https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design
**[reference]** GDC Vault (character-controller / platformer design talks): https://www.gdcvault.com

## 6. Color / visual language of toy-like bright courses

*Descriptions only — original assets to be created. Grounded in Fall Guys' stated vinyl-toy character aesthetic and the game-show DNA.*

**Verified design intent (Fall Guys Wikipedia):** character designs were inspired by the look of **vinyl toys**, and the whole presentation aims to recreate "being on a game show." This sets the visual language: saturated, toylike, game-show-bright, with every surface and hazard readable as a distinct prop.

**Material & palette conventions:**
- **Floor/walkable:** soft matte pastel or saturated single-tone (pink, teal, lime, sky-blue). Flat shading, slight bevel, no realistic texture — reads as plastic/vinyl. Matte (not glossy) so depth and edges read cleanly.
- **Hazards (sweeper arms, bumpers):** high-contrast accent — **yellow/orange/red** with a darker rim or stripe. The leading edge of a rotating arm is often a different shade or tapered so rotation direction is instantly readable.
- **Bounce pads:** universally **yellow + coil/spring motif + arrow**; pulsing animation optional. Never floor-colored.
- **Kill zones (slime/pit):** distinct translucent liquid (Fall Guys' signature **pink/teal slime**) or a clearly different "void" color (deep purple/black). Slime is Fall Guys' canonical elimination-surface material. **[verified-live]** Wikipedia confirms "Slime" as an authored Creative material and elimination mechanic.
- **Checkpoints:** flag/banner in a stand-out color (often striped), with a visible "activated" state change (color flip / glow) so the player knows the save fired.
- **Finish:** brightest, most saturated element on the course — confetti palette (multi-color), gold crown/flag, celebration VFX. Over-signaled on purpose.
- **Background:** soft gradient sky, distant cartoon props, low-saturation so the *course* pops. Confetti/balloon ambient particles for energy without competing with hazard readability.

**Readability hierarchy (most → least saturated/contrasted):** finish > hazards > bounce pads > checkpoints > walkable floor > background. If two adjacent elements share saturation, the player can't tell floor from hazard — that's the failure mode to avoid.
**[verified-live]** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_Guys (vinyl-toy inspiration, game-show framing, slime material)
**[reference]** Fall Guys official media/news for palette reference: https://fallguys.com/news
